report.answer_text:
The decision: On September 17, 2025, the Fed cut interest rates by a quarter point. That lowered the federal funds rate to between 4% and 4.25%, down from 4.25% to 4.5%.[1] It was the first cut since December 2024.[1] The vote was 11-1.[2] The one dissenter, Stephen Miran, preferred a larger half-point cut.[3][4]
Why they did it:
A weaker job market. The Fed's statement said it cut "in light of the shift in the balance of risks," and noted that risks to employment had risen.[4] Officials were concerned that the labor market was weakening. Upside risks to inflation persisted, but they still expected inflation to ease back to the 2% target.[2]
Jobs weighed more than inflation. By cutting, the Fed signaled it saw the slowing labor market as a more pressing concern than rising prices. Chair Powell had underlined this at his Jackson Hole address the month before.[1] One analyst said the Fed saw a softening labor market as a bigger risk than potential inflation from tariffs that hadn't yet materialized.[5]
"Risk management." Powell described the cut as risk management rather than an effort to shore up a weak economy.[6] He said it put policy in a "more neutral" position than the earlier "moderately restrictive" stance.[6]
Looking ahead: The Fed's "dot plot" pointed to two more cuts before the end of 2025 and another in 2027, as rates approach a long-run neutral level of about 3%.[6] The Fed did go on to cut again in October and December 2025.[7]
Politics: The cut came amid intense political pressure, with President Trump repeatedly accusing Powell of moving too slowly to ease borrowing costs.[1] Powell and the Fed framed the decision around the economic data.
